name: Chloe Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a line cook at Stack and Shake, a brunch and burger chain restaurant in the shopping centre of a small town. On a Saturday we do about three hundred covers, pancakes and eggs until noon, then smash burgers and loaded fries. I run the griddle and I'm the one the manager calls when the new kit plays up. I like the pace and figuring things out, but the music and the fryer alarms give me a headache by four.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said new kit. What's that about?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Head office is trialling an automatic fryer at our branch, it drops and lifts the baskets itself. I picked it up faster than anyone, so now I'm the unofficial fryer person. I use AI on my phone every day, for my budget, for recipes, even to check the allergen sheet when it's confusing. I live with my partner Dev, who picks orders at the big warehouse on the ring road, and we've got about three hundred saved between us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still useful, just not magic. At work I'd say the automatic fryer is handy but it's not taking anyone's job. Online I'd say people got too excited and too scared, both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I stay where I am, which is fine but not great. The pay at Stack and Shake is low, and there's no next step unless the kitchen manager leaves. And Dev's warehouse shifts change week to week, so our money jumps around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for my own budget and the allergen checks, because it saves me time. I'd ask about the chain's shift supervisor training, since that's the only way up. And we'd keep a little buffer, maybe fifty a month, for when Dev's hours drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels fine, a bit stuck. I'm good at something that isn't going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there's no next step. How long until the kitchen manager leaves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody knows. Carl (the kitchen manager) has been there eight years and seems happy. I've hinted that I want to move up, and he says be patient. But I'm not great at patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Dev's changing shifts do to your month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some weeks he gets forty hours and some weeks twenty-two. When it's twenty-two, I'm moving money around to make rent. It's the main reason I check my banking app every morning.

say: I'd say AI is **useful but not magic**.
I'd say people got **too excited** and too scared at once.
think: I think I'd be **stuck** at low pay with no next step.
I think Dev's **changing shifts** make our money jump around.
do: Keep using **AI** for budgeting and allergen checks.
Save **fifty a month** for weeks when Dev's hours drop.
feel: She feels **fine but stuck**, good at something going nowhere.
S0.quote: I'm good at something that isn't going anywhere.
fieldNote: Chloe already runs the **automatic fryer**, the kitchen's first robot.
Her money stress comes from **Dev's warehouse shifts**.
She wants to **move up** and finds waiting hard.

steps.text: Keep using AI for budgeting and allergen checks
Apply for the chain's shift supervisor training
Save fifty a month for Dev's short weeks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for people who are willing to learn. At work I'd say let's get good at the new kit before head office brings in someone who already is. Online I'd say it's going to be tough for some, but there are new jobs too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a decent position because I'm already the fryer person. Head office will roll the kit out to other branches, and they'll need someone who can train cooks on it. But I also think the chain will want fewer cooks per shift, and I'd be competing with people I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Carl to put my name forward to train other branches on the automatic fryer. I'd do the chain's online course on their new kitchen system as soon as it's out. And I'd tell Dev to start looking at the warehouse's robot maintenance roles, because his job's more at risk than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting, mostly. A bit guilty, because I know some people on my shift won't be as lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said competing with people you like. Who do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jodie has been there longer than me but hates the screens. If the chain cuts a cook per shift, it's probably Jodie (a fellow line cook) or the new lad. I'd try to help her learn, but I'd still want my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much more would a trainer role pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a pound or two more an hour, plus travel to other branches. That's about two hundred a month, which would be our savings. It would also be my way out of the griddle.

say: I'd call it a **chance** for people willing to learn.
I'd say get good at the **new kit** before head office hires someone.
think: I think I'm well placed as the **fryer person**.
I think the chain will want **fewer cooks** per shift.
do: Ask Carl to put her forward as an **equipment trainer**.
Take the chain's **online course** on the new kitchen system.
Urge Dev to look at **robot maintenance** roles.
feel: She feels **mostly excited**, with some **guilt** about workmates.
S1.quote: If the chain cuts a cook per shift, it's probably Jodie (a fellow line cook) or the new lad.
fieldNote: Chloe sees **training others** on kit as her way up.
She's honest about **competing** with workmates she likes.
She sees **Dev's warehouse job** as more exposed than her own.

steps.text: Ask Carl to nominate her as the fryer trainer for other branches

Help Dev apply for warehouse robot maintenance roles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough, so learn everything you can right now. At work I'd tell people to stop pretending it won't come here. Online I'd say governments should help people retrain, quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think 2028 takes out head office first, the planning and ordering and marketing. Then the robots come for the kitchen about 2031, and that includes my griddle. I'd be the one who knows the machines, which is good, but how many machine people does a chain need?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a proper course in kitchen equipment repair, so I'm useful when things break. I'd push to get on the chain's rollout team, because that's travel and better pay. And Dev and I would save hard, maybe skip our holiday, to get three months' rent in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a race. I'm a fast runner, but with AGI by 2028 the track is short. Anxious, honestly, but I'd be moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my window, basically. In those three years the chain is buying robots and needs people to set them up and fix them. After 2031, the robots might need fewer of us, so I'd want to be on the repair side by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dev the night this was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're doing this together, both of us learn something technical this year. He'd say he's tired, and he'd be right, warehouse work is brutal. But I'd push, because his job goes even faster than mine.

say: I'd tell people at work to **learn everything** they can right now.
I'd say governments should **fund retraining** quickly, before the robots arrive.
think: I think **head office** goes first in 2028, then my griddle around 2031.
I think a chain needs only a few **machine people**.
do: Take a course in **kitchen equipment repair**.
Skip the holiday to save **three months' rent**.
feel: She feels **anxious but moving**, like a fast runner on a short track.
S2.quote: I'm a fast runner, but with AGI by 2028 the track is short.
fieldNote: Chloe treats the **three-year gap** as her window to move into repairs.
She's clear that machine jobs will be **few**.
She pushes **Dev** to retrain alongside her.

steps.text: Enrol in a kitchen equipment repair course
Apply to join the chain's robot rollout team
Skip this year's holiday to save three months' rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead, if you start now. At work I'd say learn the kit, learn the screens, don't wait. Online I'd share any training offers I find, because people don't know what's out there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one suits me. Thinking AI by 2031, robots about 2034, gives me time to become the person who fixes the kitchen robots. I'd be thirty-five, still young enough to start something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an evening course in equipment repair and use AI to help me learn faster. I'd volunteer for every new kit trial at Stack and Shake. And I'd set up a direct debit to savings, sixty a month, so it happens without me thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels mostly good, with some worry about money. I'm the sort who likes a clear target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the kitchen altogether?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, if repair work pays better and lasts longer. I like cooking, but I like having a future more. My nan would be horrified, she thinks cooks are artists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the chain shuts the branch before then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go wherever the repair work is, even if it means moving to the city. Dev would come, his warehouse has a city branch. I'd hate leaving my mum, but I'd do it.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to get ahead** if you start now.
I'd share every **training offer** I find online with my workmates.
think: I think this one **suits me** best.
I think I can become the person who **fixes kitchen robots**.
do: Volunteer for every **new kit trial** at Stack and Shake.
Set up a **sixty-a-month** direct debit to savings.
feel: She feels **mostly good**, with some worry about money.
S3.quote: I like cooking, but I like having a future more.
fieldNote: Chloe would **leave cooking** for repair work without much regret.
She'd **move to the city** if the branch closed.
Her **nan's view** of cooks as artists shows a family pull she resists.

steps.text: Start an evening equipment repair course
Volunteer for every new kitchen kit trial
Set up a sixty-a-month savings direct debit
Move to the city with Dev if the branch closes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for not getting ready. At work I'd keep pushing people to learn the new kit. Online I'd say the slow version is the one where we can actually plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd cook until about 2039, so nearly forty. By then I want to be running a kitchen or fixing them. The thinking AI coming first would help me plan menus and costs if I'm a manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for kitchen manager in the next few years and use AI for rotas and stock. I'd do the equipment repair course over two years, steadily. And Dev and I would start saving for a deposit on a small place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels good. Uneasy about money, as always, but I'd feel ahead of things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ahead of things. Is there any risk you'd relax too much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, I do get bored easily. Boredom makes me try new things, not sit still. My risk is more the opposite, I'd chase too many courses. I'd need to pick one and stick with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a deposit mean for you and Dev?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would mean stopping renting, which feels like throwing money away. We'd need maybe ten thousand, which is a lot on our wages. But with ten years, if we both moved up, maybe.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse** for not getting ready.
I'd call the slow version the one where we **can plan**.
think: I think I'd cook until about **2039**, nearly forty.
I think thinking AI would help me as a **kitchen manager**.
do: Go for **kitchen manager** in the next few years.
Do the **repair course** steadily over two years.
Save for a **house deposit** with Dev.
feel: She feels **good and ahead**, though money still nags.
S4.quote: Boredom makes me try new things, not sit still.
fieldNote: Chloe aims to **run or fix** kitchens by forty.
She knows her risk is **chasing too many courses**.
A **ten-thousand** house deposit is her long-term goal.

steps.text: Apply for kitchen manager at Stack and Shake within three years
Use AI for rotas and stock as manager
Save toward a ten-thousand-pound house deposit with Dev

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the window would be so short and Dev's job goes even faster than mine. What would help is cheap evening courses in repair and tech, and some help with rent while people retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples. Dev and I are both exposed in different ways, and we plan together. Facing AI isn't one person's problem for us, it's two people sharing one thin bank account.

headlineQuote: Facing AI isn't one person's problem for us, it's two people sharing one thin bank account.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old line cook** at a busy brunch and burger chain.
She uses **AI daily** and runs the trial automatic fryer.
She lives with Dev, a **warehouse picker**, and they have little saved.
She wants to **move up** into training, repair or management.
Her mood stays **uneasy to anxious**, because she feels ahead but money is thin.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most, with a short window and Dev's job at risk.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **cheap evening courses** in repair and help with **rent** while retraining.
